explanation: The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It descends between the medial pterygoid and mandible, then passes anterior to the hyoglossus muscle into the floor of the mouth. It receives the chorda tympani (carrying taste and parasympathetic fibers) and provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and lingual gingiva.
keyConcept: Lingual nerve (CN V3) provides general sensation to anterior two-thirds of tongue and receives chorda tympani.
modelAnswer: The lingual nerve is a sensory branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It descends between the medial pterygoid and mandible, then passes anterior to the hyoglossus muscle into the floor of the mouth. In the infratemporal fossa, it is joined by the chorda tympani (VA VII) which carries taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of tongue and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion. The lingual nerve provides general sensation (pain, temperature, touch) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and lingual gingiva of the mandible.

explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve is the largest branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It enters the mandibular foramen and runs within the mandibular canal, giving off dental branches to all lower teeth and terminating as the mental nerve which provides sensation to the chin and lower lip.
keyConcept: Inferior alveolar nerve supplies all lower teeth via dental branches and ends as mental nerve.
modelAnswer: Branches of the inferior alveolar nerve include: (1) Mylohyoid nerve—a motor branch given off before entering the mandibular foramen, supplying the mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric. (2) Dental branches—supplying the pulp of all lower teeth (incisors, canines, premolars, and molars). (3) Interdental branches—supplying the interdental gingiva and periodontal ligaments. (4) Mental nerve—terminal branch emerging through the mental foramen to supply the skin and mucous membrane of the chin and lower lip. (5) Incisive branch—continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve anteriorly to supply lower incisors and canines.

explanation: The maxillary nerve (CN V2) is the second division of the trigeminal nerve. It leaves the trigeminal ganglion through the foramen rotundum and gives branches in the pterygopalatine fossa, infraorbital canal, and face. It carries general somatic sensation from the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, upper teeth, palate, and nasal cavity.
keyConcept: Maxillary nerve (CN V2) branches include zygomatic, pterygopalatine, posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, and palatine nerves.
modelAnswer: Branches of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) include: in the cranial cavity—middle meningeal nerve (recurrent branch); in the pterygopalatine fossa—zygomatic nerve, greater and lesser palatine nerves, nasopalatine nerve, posterior superior alveolar nerve, and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion; in the infraorbital canal—anterior and middle superior alveolar nerves; terminal branches on the face—infraorbital nerve dividing into inferior palpebral, external nasal, and superior labial branches.

explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3) that arises by two roots encircling the middle meningeal artery. It supplies sensory innervation to the temple, temporomandibular joint, external auditory meatus, and tympanic membrane. It also carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3) supplies temple, TMJ, external ear, and carries parasympathetic fibers to parotid gland.
modelAnswer: Branches of the auriculotemporal nerve include: (1) Articular branches—to the temporomandibular joint. (2) Parotid branches—carrying postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. (3) Anterior auricular branches—to the skin of the auricle. (4) Branches to the external auditory meatus—supplying skin and tympanic membrane. (5) Superficial temporal branches—terminal branches supplying the skin of the temple and scalp.

explanation: The infraorbital nerve is the terminal branch of the maxillary nerve (CN V2) that emerges through the infraorbital foramen. It provides sensory innervation to the lower eyelid, side of the nose, upper lip, and upper labial gingiva. Its branches within the infraorbital canal include the anterior and middle superior alveolar nerves.
keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (CN V2) divides into inferior palpebral, external nasal, and superior labial branches.
modelAnswer: The infraorbital nerve gives the following branches: within the infraorbital canal—anterior superior alveolar nerve (to upper incisors and canines) and middle superior alveolar nerve (to upper premolars); terminal branches on the face—inferior palpebral branches (to lower eyelid), external nasal branches (to ala and vestibule of nose), and superior labial branches (to upper lip and labial gingiva).

explanation: The pterygopalatine fossa is a small pyramidal space between the pterygopalatine fissure posteriorly, the orbit anteriorly, the nasal cavity medially, and the infratemporal fossa laterally. It contains the maxillary nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion, and terminal branches of the maxillary artery.
keyConcept: Pterygopalatine fossa communicates with orbit, nasal cavity, infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, and pharynx.
modelAnswer: Boundaries of the pterygopalatine fossa: anterior—maxilla (posterior surface); posterior—pterygoid process and greater wing of sphenoid (with foramen rotundum superiorly, pterygoid canal inferiorly); medial—perpendicular plate of palatine bone with sphenopalatine foramen; lateral—pterygomaxillary fissure opening into infratemporal fossa; superior—orbital process of palatine bone with inferior orbital fissure; inferior—pyramidal process of palatine bone with greater and lesser palatine foramina. It communicates with the orbit, nasal cavity, infratemporal fossa, middle cranial fossa, and pharynx.

explanation: The maxillary artery is a terminal branch of the external carotid artery that supplies deep structures of the face, jaws, nasal cavity, and cranial dura. It is divided into three parts by the lateral pterygoid muscle.
keyConcept: Maxillary artery has three parts: mandibular (1st), pterygoid (2nd), and pterygopalatine (3rd).
modelAnswer: Branches of the maxillary artery: First (mandibular) part—deep auricular, anterior tympanic, middle meningeal, accessory meningeal, and inferior alveolar arteries. Second (pterygoid) part—masseteric, pterygoid, buccal, and deep temporal arteries. Third (pterygopalatine) part—posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater palatine, lesser palatine, nasopalatine, sphenopalatine, and artery of pterygoid canal.

explanation: The pterygoid plexus of veins is a network of veins located around the lateral and medial pterygoid muscles in the infratemporal fossa. It receives tributaries from the deep facial vein, middle meningeal veins, sphenopalatine veins, and branches corresponding to the maxillary artery. It drains via the maxillary vein into the retromandibular vein.
keyConcept: Pterygoid plexus connects maxillary veins to cavernous sinus via emissary veins.
modelAnswer: The pterygoid plexus of veins is located in the infratemporal fossa around the pterygoid muscles. It receives tributaries corresponding to the branches of the maxillary artery (deep temporal, pterygoid, masseteric, buccal, middle meningeal, inferior alveolar veins), the sphenopalatine vein, and veins from the nasal cavity and palate. It communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins through the foramen lacerum, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum. It drains posteriorly into the maxillary vein, which continues as the retromandibular vein.
